Occasionally, the world encounters a genius – someone who overcomes a challenge no one else could. Yi Sun-sin was such a man, and the crisis he solved saved Joseon.

Yi was born in 1545 into a family that had fallen upon hard times. His grandfather had been a Confucian scholar caught up in the purges of Sarim – Confucian scholars that stood in opposition to monarchical power. Blacklisted from the heights that normally would have been open to their aristocratic station, the Yi family retreated to an unobtrusive role, well outside of politics. Despite this poor fortune, their commitment to Confucian ideals did not waver, and throughout his life, Yi Sun-sin proved the ideal of a Confucian man, devoted to duty and to family. Though his relationship with politics would remain volatile, his best friend, Yu Seongnyong, was an administrator who later penned an account of this period, The Book of Corrections. Yu was a friend who never lost faith in Yi, using his own connections several times to boost Yi’s fortunes and, it turns out, Korea’s fortunes as well.

Yi passed his exams for military service at the age of thirty-one and was stationed on Korea’s northern frontier, where the Jurchen people (who would later become the Manchu, the rulers of Qing China) lived and raided along the Korean borders. Here, he became known for his boldness – one story has him defending an ambush on a border fort from a massive Jurchen raid with a crew of only twelve Korean soldiers. Key, too, in this story is his skill at archery, especially the yuyeopjeon – faster, short-range arrows. Following his success, Yi’s friend Yu took the opportunity to appoint Yi from a regional commander to the head of the Joseon navy – a meteoric rise that bypassed the expected trajectory of advancement.

When Yi took over the navy, he found it in a state of extreme disarray, far from prepared to defend against Korean foes. A period of peace as a tributary of Ming China had lured the government into complacency. Meanwhile, Korea’s other neighbor Japan had an ambitious new ruler, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who had set his sights on China. Korea was caught in the middle, and Yi began preparing the navy for conflict.

One of Yi’s legacies is his use of turtle ships. While an earlier version of the ships had seen use over a century earlier (the gwiseon, as they were called), they had long been abandoned by the time of Yi’s admiralship. Recognizing the tactical gaps of the Japanese navy which relied on boarding ships to win naval battles, Yi developed improvements for the turtle ship and deployed them to great effect. The ships were highly agile, were armed with a variety of cannons, and had a layer of spikes to resist attempts at boarding. The result was masterful.

The Japanese invaded Korea in 1592 and quickly swept in, occupying most of its settlements, including the capital, but control of the Korean coasts proved far less simple. Over the course of the war, Yi proved a brilliant admiral despite having had no naval warfare experience beforehand. In the first campaign, with a fleet composed mostly of fishing boats, Admiral Yi destroyed dozens of Japanese ships without losing a single vessel. Later that year, he used a clever feint with only a few ships to coax a much larger Japanese force out of their defensive location and then turned his ships and rained fire on his enemies, destroying or capturing over 50 vessels.

Though Yi’s clever strategies kept the Japanese from fully dominating Korea, his true enemies were his own fellow Koreans. Buffeted by jealous colleagues and inept administrators (whom he refused to obey), Yi was stripped of his post and imprisoned, narrowly escaping a death sentence. In Yi’s place, the admiral of the fleet was Won Gyun, one of Yi’s former captains and, according to Yi’s own writings, a cowardly, sniveling man. He proved as incapable as Yi believed him, losing 137 of 150 warships to a Japanese ambush, with tens of thousands of his men massacred. Once again, with the Korean navy diminished to a pitiful point and Toyotomi threatening on the doorstep, the Korean court rethought its earlier position and called on Yi Sun-sin to save them. He was reinstated as admiral of the fleet and quickly set to work.

With only 13 ships, the Korean navy was largely outnumbered by the Japanese fleet. Nonetheless, Yi lured the Japanese into a dangerous strait at Myeongyang and straight into an ambush. With odds nearly 25 to 1, Yi managed to defeat the Japanese navy in one of history’s most brilliant examples of naval warfare. Toyotomi made a final attempt to invade Korea and his forces were defeated at Noryang at the tail end of 1598. Alas, a stray bullet caught Yi Sun-sin in this final battle, and he died. His men and the people of Korea mourned him, recognizing that he was the reason they remained free from a Japanese yoke.

Yi is remembered as a master of naval strategy. Despite having no formal training in naval matters, he used Korea’s rocky coast and its will to resist to lead the Joseon navy from improbable success to success. He is remembered alongside Horatio Nelson and other naval commanders as a model of determination, wisdom, and victory.
Those who seek death shall live, and those who seek life shall die.
I am Yi Sun-sin. Let us play a game of baduk so I may see what you're about.

My dreams show a portent. You as a fish on a skewer.
Your haste will be your ruin. Better to be prudent like a mountain.
These currents have bested me. What now? I am lost at sea and forgotten.
A wise strategy steels the heart for what comes.
One may as well entrust a fish to a cat.
The sailing moon is clear and bright. Fair skies tomorrow and a rest well-earned.

Though the numbers may be against you, Admiral Yi, you build your plans following the currents and tides. The great wave may darken the horizon, but like the rocks of Myeongnyang, when it breaks, you will remain - implacable, unmovable, unwilling to surrender. Take up your post, and hold your people fast against the tide.

The voices of the {1_CIVILIZATION_ADJ} people echo with hope for the future; Yi Sun-sin knows he must ensure their good fortune. The coasts are bountiful yet vulnerable. Duty demands a plan for defense.
Build a fleet to safeguard the shore.
Free Promotion on current Fleet Commanders.
{1_CIVILIZATION_ADJ} ships ensure the safety of the people.
Study the strategies of the great masters.
The art of war requires a ready mind.
Build a Library and Research 2 Technology Masteries.

As envious neighbors set their sights on the {1_CIVILIZATION_ADJ} coasts, Yi Sun-sin evaluates the fleet. Sound vessels are only one part of a successful navy; its admirals too must be disciplined leaders. Such men are few and valuable.
Reward the best with a rare commendation.
A steadfast admiral is worth more than one hundred ships.
Have a Fleet Commander with a Commendation.
The sea will sort the cowards from the brave.
Yi Sun-sin's sailors have mapped the sea against the stars. Yet the rocky coasts have no reflection in the sky, and shoals do not distinguish between friend and foe.
With more study, we can further our advantage.
The coasts are a harbor for the fleet and a snare for enemies.
Research Navigation Mastery and Build a Lighthouse.
The cape is a familiar face to {1_CIVILIZATION_ADJ} sailors.

A hostile neighbor is making a mockery of {1_civilization_adj} borders. The troops are eager to march, but Admiral Yi must choose the gate of their departure to ensure success of the mission. West, the element of metal, represents destruction; east, the element of wood, signifies cooperation.
West. This is a mission of force.

Gossip about a captain’s misbehavior is on everyone’s lips in Yi Sun-sin’s court. A peer has accused the captain of disobeying the admiral’s orders for a full assault, but the captain defends his choice to harry instead. He claims the orders would have led his men straight into an ambush.
{1_reward}, but Fleet Commander is returned to Owned Territory.
Yi Sun-sin looks out across the dark waves to the distant horizon. What lies beyond the familiar shores? Perhaps it is time to brave the depths.
The fleet chafes for new challenges.
New horizons excite the curiosity of {1_CIVILIZATION_ADJ} scholars.
Lately, the seas swarm with enemy warships escorting convoys of valuable resources. Yi Sun-sin's fleet stands ready to claim this treasure, for the seas belong to the bold.
The sea itself is a treasure worth protecting.
The avarice of others is a constant menace, but Yi Sun-sin is never caught unawares. While neighbors vie for dominance, he sets his sights on treasure afar. The admirals must be ready to press ahead.
The path of duty demands action.
A disciplined admiral knows when to seize the advantage.
Have a Fleet Commander with 2 Commendations.
Young scholars walk the streets of {1_capital}, filling the air with questions and curiosity. Their ideas are promising, but Yi Sun-sin recognizes that true progress requires diverse perspectives.
Attract more scholars to expand the nexus of learning.
The mind may be nimble, but might wins in the end.

{1_CIVILIZATION_ADJ} scholars are among the first to step foot on distant shores. New materials spur invention, and newly-met neighbors exchange fresh ideas. Yi Sun-sin sees the potential of this developing frontier.
Cultivate a hub of learning amidst the new environs.
The quest for new knowledge benefits {1_CIVILIZATION_ADJ} society at home and abroad.

A lacquered box, found in the captain’s quarters of the enemy’s ship, contains a golden fan. It bears the name of their leader, Toyotomi Hideyoshi. A gift, perhaps. Yi Sun-sin scoffs at the extravagant and useless trinket.
The enemy’s fleet vastly outnumbers Yi Sun-sin’s own force, yet his clever strategies have given him a foothold. Now to set the trap.
Feint a retreat to draw them out.
With a grieving heart, Yi Sun-sin returns to his base, one less comrade to share the evening cups with. The sinking moon shines on the grim faces of his crew. Few will sleep well tonight.
Build a shrine to pay respects.
Memorialize him with an archery ground.

Intelligence reports tell Yi Sun-sin that this bold samurai had planned to unify the realm and steal the land of his neighbors. So much for dreams of grandeur. The promising warlord lies broken now, his arrogance a useless prop against a stronger foe.
Harmony is a greater goal than conquest.

As the battle rages, Yi Sun-sin glimpses a standard floating amidst the flotsam. Quickly, he urges a sailor to haul it in. Dragged through the waves, the standard slips to reveal a face. As Yi Sun-sin had suspected, it is the enemy commander, or at least what is left of him, the standard now his shroud.
May he find peace under the waves.
No longer are the seas solely ruled by ships – vessels of the sky now too hold sway. Duty demands an answer, and Yi Sun-sin is prepared.
Bridge the sea and the sky to ensure a safe border.
Across sea and sky, the path of duty leads ever onward.
Have an Aircraft Carrier with a Commendation.

{1_CIVILIZATION_ADJ} scientists announce to Yi Sun-sin that they have harnessed lightning. What limit can there be to knowledge when the sky is bottled in a bulb? The very air is thick with possibility.
The night awash in light is just the beginning.
The frontier of knowledge climbs ever higher.

As the enemy’s turtle ship sinks beneath the waves, Yi Sun-sin marvels at the design. Truly, some genius must have invented such a vessel, able to bombard and maneuver while deftly fending off enemy fire. Perhaps the {1_civilization_adj} engineers could develop a counter.
Develop a schematic with the engineers.
Our fleet is already more than capable.

Late in the afternoon, a patrol ship brings messages from the mainland. One weathered soldier gasps at the bad news - his long-sick mother has passed. In Yi Sun-sin’s cabin, he requests a leave of absence, pressing on his duty to family.
His duty is with his troops.
Xiao is the most important virtue.

Confucian scholarship and Joseon history combine amidst the beauty of the city’s monuments. Inspired by the sights, Yi Sun-sin declares the foundation of Kyujanggak, a place to preserve and spread the knowledge of Joseon excellence.
Confucian ideals will be known to all.
Science is the key to our future.
